client: I've been really struggling lately with this huge group project I got assigned at university. There's going to be a presentation at the end of it, and just thinking about standing up in front of everyone makes my chest tight and my mind go completely blank. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the presentation is still going to happen whether I feel better about it or not.
therapist: What you're describing — that tightness in your chest, your mind going blank — those are really real and uncomfortable experiences, and I can hear in your voice a kind of quiet exhaustion, like you're carrying this weight but almost holding your breath around it. You're right that the presentation won't disappear, but what *can* change is how your mind and body relate to it — and that's actually where we have more power than it might feel like right now. Would you be open to exploring what specific thoughts are showing up when you imagine standing in front of that group, so we can start to look at them together?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess when I picture it, the main thought is that everyone's going to see me freeze up and think I'm completely incompetent, like I don't belong there. And then I start worrying that my group members will be embarrassed by me, which makes me feel guilty on top of everything else. I'm willing to talk about it, but I honestly don't see how naming the thoughts is going to make them feel less true in the moment when I'm actually standing there.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, almost like the thoughts are tumbling out before you can stop them — tells me this fear feels very alive and urgent for you, not just abstract worry. That thought, "I'll freeze and they'll see I don't belong," is a really painful one, and it makes complete sense that it feels *true* rather than just a fear. What CBT helps us do isn't make the thought disappear in the moment, but build enough evidence *beforehand* that when it shows up, you have something solid to hold onto — so I'd love to gently ask: what's the actual evidence, from your experience, that you *do* belong there?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I mean, I did get accepted into the program like everyone else, and I've done okay on individual assignments. But when I'm actually in that moment, none of that feels real or relevant — it's like my brain just completely discards all of it and zeroes in on every time I've stumbled over my words or looked awkward. I guess I can see what you're trying to do, but I'm worried that in the actual moment, the anxiety is just going to be louder than any list of evidence I've built up beforehand.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly but very quickly, like part of you is rushing to get ahead of the hope before it can disappoint you — actually tells me something important: you *can* see the evidence, you're just scared to trust it. And that's one of the most honest things a person can say. You've actually just identified the real target for our work — it's not about building a longer list, it's about practicing *returning* to that evidence when anxiety tries to hijack it, which is a skill we can genuinely rehearse together before you're ever standing at that podium.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: That actually... lands a bit differently than I expected, the part about being scared to trust it rather than just not having enough evidence. I think that's probably true, but I'm not sure what "rehearsing returning to it" actually looks like in practice — like, is that something I'd do alone, or with you, and would it actually feel different from just telling myself to calm down, which never works? I guess I'm a little skeptical but also maybe slightly more open than I was when I walked in here.
therapist: That slight openness you're naming — even alongside the skepticism — is actually really significant, and I can hear it in your voice too, a kind of cautious curiosity that feels different from where you started. What we'd do together is very different from "just calm down," because instead of suppressing the anxiety, we'd practice *noticing* the thought, acknowledging it, and then deliberately redirecting your attention to something grounded and true — almost like a mental muscle we build together first, so it's familiar when you need it most. We'd do it here with me, in low-stakes moments, so that by the time you're at that podium, your brain has already done it enough times that it feels like a path it knows how to take.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: The "mental muscle" idea makes a bit more sense to me than just reciting a list of facts to myself, I'll admit that. But I'm already thinking about how my group members are going to be watching me practice or something, and whether doing it in here with you is really going to translate to standing in front of an actual audience with real stakes. I suppose my biggest fear is that I'll do all this work and then still freeze up on the day, and then I'll feel even worse because I tried and it still didn't help.
therapist: There's something really telling in how you just said that — your voice is moving quickly, almost like you're trying to outrun the hope before it can let you down, and underneath the worry I can hear something that sounds almost like cautious investment, like part of you *wants* this to work even as another part is bracing for disappointment. That fear — "I'll try and it still won't be enough" — is actually one of the most important things we could work with, because it's the same all-or-nothing thinking that shows up in the presentation itself: either it goes perfectly or it proves you don't belong. What if "freezing briefly but recovering" could count as success — would your brain allow that, or does it only accept perfect?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, my brain definitely only accepts perfect, and hearing you say that out loud makes me realize how exhausting that standard actually is. I can intellectually see that recovering from a stumble is better than not trying at all, but I genuinely don't know if I'd feel that way in the moment — I think I'd still walk away replaying every second of it and feeling like I'd failed my group. It's weird because part of me wants to believe "brief freeze then recover" could be enough, but another part of me is already arguing back that my group members wouldn't see it that way.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, almost carefully, like you're handling something fragile — matches exactly what you're describing: a part of you that's genuinely tired of carrying that perfectionist standard, but speaking very gently around it, as if saying it too loudly might make it worse. That thought, "my group members wouldn't see it that way," is worth pausing on — because right now it feels like a fact, but it's actually a prediction your anxious mind is making on their behalf, without any real evidence. What would it mean to gently ask yourself: is that what they'd actually think, or is that the perfectionist part of you projecting its own harsh standard onto them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: When you put it that way, I think I probably am projecting, because honestly my group members have never actually said anything harsh to me — I'm basically writing their reactions before they've even happened. But it's hard to just switch that off, because the projection feels so convincing in the moment, like it's protecting me from being blindsided rather than just making things worse. I guess I'm wondering how I'm supposed to catch myself doing that in real time when the anxiety is already running the show.
therapist: The way your voice sounds right now — high and a little stretched, like you're reaching for something just out of grasp — reflects exactly what you're describing: you can *see* the projection clearly from here, but you're genuinely uncertain how to catch it when anxiety is already in the driver's seat, and that's not a personal failing, that's just how anxiety works. The key isn't stopping the projection before it starts, but building a small, simple "pattern interrupt" — one grounding question you can practice now until it becomes automatic, something like "is this a fact or a forecast?" — so that even mid-anxiety, there's a familiar hook your mind can catch. We'd work on making that question feel almost reflexive together, so it doesn't require you to be calm first in order to use it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: "Is this a fact or a forecast?" is actually simple enough that I can imagine remembering it, which is more than I can say for some of the other things I've tried before. But I'm a little worried that in the moment I'll ask myself that question and then just answer "well it feels like a fact" and be right back where I started. I suppose I'm willing to try practicing it here though, even if I'm not fully convinced yet that it'll stick when the real pressure is on.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, with a kind of bright tension in your voice — tells me that even as you're offering to try, there's still a part of you bracing, almost like you're waiting to be proven right that it won't work. And that's actually the perfect thing to notice, because when you ask "is this a fact or a forecast?" and your mind answers "it feels like a fact," that's not the question failing — that's the question *working*, because you've just caught your brain doing exactly what we're talking about. Feelings of certainty aren't the same as evidence, and that's the next layer we'd practice: not just asking the question, but gently following it with "what would I need to actually *know* this is true, rather than just feel it?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That reframe actually catches me off guard a bit — the idea that my brain answering "it feels like a fact" is the question working rather than failing is genuinely not how I expected that to go. I think what makes me nervous about the follow-up question, "what would I need to actually know this is true," is that I'm worried I'd just spiral into trying to find proof, and that search would make the anxiety worse rather than better. But I can see there's something different about asking for evidence versus just sitting inside the feeling, so I'm cautiously willing to try it out here with you where it feels a bit safer.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — very softly but incredibly quickly, like your thoughts are moving faster than you can quite hold onto them — tells me that even as you're opening a door, there's still a quiet nervousness underneath, almost like you're stepping forward while watching carefully for the floor to give way. That worry about spiraling into proof-seeking is actually really important, because the goal of "what would I need to know this is true" isn't to launch an investigation — it's just a gentle pause, a moment to notice that certainty and truth aren't the same thing, and then let the thought loosen its grip rather than tighten it. So let's try it together right now, safely: pick one of those forecasts about your group members, and we'll just sit with that question for a moment — not to solve it, just to see what happens when you don't have to treat the feeling as the final answer.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Okay, so the forecast I keep coming back to is that if I stumble during the presentation, my group members are going to be quietly furious with me and think they'd have been better off without me. When I ask myself what I'd actually need to know that's true, I guess I realize I'd need them to have actually said something like that, or given me a real sign — and they haven't, not once. It's strange because just saying that out loud doesn't make the feeling go away, but it does feel slightly less like a wall and more like... I don't know, something I made up and then forgot I made up.
therapist: What you just did — that's not a small thing, even if it doesn't feel dramatic, and I notice your voice is still moving very quickly and sitting quite high, like part of you is still a little breathless from the realisation. "Something I made up and then forgot I made up" is honestly one of the most precise descriptions of anxious forecasting I've heard, and the fact that the feeling didn't vanish but the wall softened slightly — that *is* what progress actually feels like, it's rarely a sudden silence, it's usually exactly that: a loosening. You've just used the question in real time and found something true on the other side of it, which means your brain now has one genuine experience of it working, and that's the first thread of that mental muscle we were talking about.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
